chunks: From him, from Safwan, from Ibn Sinan, who said:
I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the child of fornication: is he bought, employed, and sold? He said, 'Yes.'
Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Umar ibn Udhaynah, who said:

I wrote to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) asking him about a man who had wood and sold it to one who would make bindings (for barrels) from it; he said, 'There is no harm with it.' And about a man who had wood and sold it to one who would make beams (for doors) from it; he said, 'No.'

key_terms.لَا بَأْسَ بِهِ: There is no harm with it (permissible)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on selling wood when the buyer intends to use it for a specific purpose?
ai.summary: This excerpt from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* illustrates the application of *gharar* (uncertainty) and *mujazafa* (speculation) in commercial transactions, a key theme in Chapter 9. The first ruling confirms the marketability of *walad al-zina* as a distinct legal category of slave, while the second demonstrates how the buyer's intended use (bindings vs. beams) affects the validity of the sale, likely due to potential defects or ambiguity in the wood's suitability for structural purposes.
